newsitem.title: UKRAINE: FOCUS - Big Ukraine - IMF deal expected soon.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Big Ukraine - IMF deal expected soon.

text.p: Ukraine is expected to announce in the next few days an agreement in principle on a new multi-billion dollar loan programme with the International Monetary Fund (IMF), sources close to the talks said on Monday.
"It sounds like they've made their breakthrough," said one economist.

An IMF mission completed a three-week visit to Kiev on Friday to negotiate a three-year, $2.5-3.0 billion Extended Fund Facility (EFF), which would succeed the $867 million stand-by programme when it runs out early next year.

IMF Resident Representative Alex Sundakov said the Fund's board, due to meet in Washington next month, would decide whether to approve the next tranche of the stand-by programme, usually in the amount of $100 million.
He would not comment on the EFF.

Sources close to the talks, noting that the two sides extended the mission's visit by a week as they wrangled over Ukraine's wish to increase its 1997 budget deficit, said an agreement would be announced shortly.
"I understand that Ukraine was successful in getting a slightly higher deficit target," said the economist.

Ukraine said last week that it planned to raise the 1997 budget deficit to 5.8 percent of gross domestic product, or four percent by Western calculations, from an initially proposed 3.8 percent of GDP, or three percent by Western calculations.
"It seems that the IMF agreed to increase the deficit levels if Ukraine used non-inflationary financing. It could be external, or internal through the Treasury bill market," another economist said.
The 1997 draft budget, which predicts Ukraine's first growth since it achieved independence in 1991 and 25 percent annual inflation, is currently before parliament.
GDP contracted further this year, after falling 11.8 percent in 1995. Inflation for 1996 is forecast at about 40 percent.
An economist said the IMF would attach a "line of conditionality" stating that the budget must fall into line with IMF requirements if Ukraine hopes to receive EFF money.

President Leonid Kuchma said last week that he would refuse to sign an "unrealistic" budget, indicating he would be prepared to fight hard against the left-dominated parliament if it did not support the government's proposed budget.
The budget must be passed by January 1 under the terms of Ukraine's new constitution.

The government has not released details on how it will cover the deficit, though the original draft split payment almost evenly between foreign credits and Treasury-bill revenues. Ukraine has also announced it will issue foreign bonds in 1997.
One of the economists said final approval for the EFF would come in December or even in January, when the IMF board has scheduled meetings.
Ukraine had requested a stabilisation fund for the hryvnia currency, which was introduced in September, as part of the EFF.
"Ukraine also has to decide on an exchange rate regime, and there are no official decisions on that," one economist said.
